findings.derivation: run_python on the R01 CSV: each sample holds its value until the next (no gap exceeds 1 s); sum of holds with frequency_hz < 49 over 16:52:30 <= t < 16:58:00 BST = 33 s. Same window with frequency_hz <= 49: 34 s. Linear interpolation: below 49 Hz from 16:53:40.000 to 16:54:13.964 = 33.964 s.

quantity.basis: count of 1-s samples strictly below 49 Hz x 1 s (zero-order hold)

findings.statement: The frequency was strictly below 49 Hz in 33 consecutive 1-s samples, 16:53:41 to 16:54:13 BST inclusive: 33 s under a zero-order hold (each sample held until the next), with no missing samples between 16:52:30 and 16:58:00. The convention matters at the boundary: 16:53:40 is exactly 49.000 Hz, so counting samples at or below 49 Hz gives 34 s, and linear interpolation between samples gives about 33.96 s.

R01 holds one published value per second (3900 rows, 16:40:00 to 17:44:59 BST) with explicit +01:00 (BST) offsets and no missing or duplicate seconds; the values are unchanged from the NESO dataset, which the publisher corrected in February 2020.

Sub-second behaviour, including the exact instants at which the frequency crossed 49 Hz or 48.8 Hz, cannot be determined from R01's 1-s samples, which record nothing between consecutive samples. The 33 s is a sample-based duration under the stated convention (strictly below 49 Hz, zero-order hold), not a measured crossing-to-crossing time.

report.executive_summary: Partial investigation covering the frequency record only. From the R01 1-s series: first minimum 49.083 Hz at 16:52:59 BST, event minimum 48.787 Hz at 16:53:49, first sample at or above 50 Hz 50.001 Hz at 16:57:16, and 33 s strictly below 49 Hz [F20, F21, F22, F23]. Sub-second crossings are not resolvable [F24, F25]. The initiating event, the generator trips and their causes were not examined.
